briefs.08234779c801fccc: The question asks whether the first published FRED ICSA value for the week ending 2026-11-28 is strictly above 189,000; a first print of exactly 189,000 resolves No. FRED shows 189,000 for the week ending 2026-11-21, updated 2026-11-25, with the next release on 2026-12-03 (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/ICSA). That advance figure was well below a consensus of about 200,000, and the prior week was revised from 203,000 to 202,000; the four-week average was 196,000 (https://www.financecalendar.com/event/us-initial-jobless-claims-november-25-2026/, 2026-11-27). The first print for the week ending 2026-11-14 was 203,000, up 1,000 (https://stockanalysis.com/news/jobless-claims-rise-third-week-november-2026/, 2026-11-19). Base rate from the latest FRED vintage (not first prints): 3,095 of 3,125 weeks since 1967 were above 189,000 (99.0%), 880 of 882 since 2010 (99.8%), and 50 of 52 over the past year (96.2%); exactly 189,000 occurred in 2 of the last 52 weeks. These counts understate the chance of a low print because they use revised data and ignore the threshold sitting at the current reading. What is different this time: the threshold equals the latest print, so the question is mostly whether the sharp drop from about 202,000 persists or reverts toward the 196,000 four-week average. The week ending 2026-11-28 contains Thanksgiving, and holiday seasonal adjustment can distort the figure; an unverified search summary says the comparable 2025 week fell to 191,000, still 2,000 above this threshold (https://angrybearblog.com/2025/12/jobless-claims-holiday-seasonality-enters-in-a-big-way, not opened). The DOL page notes technical database issues that could affect data timing (https://oui.doleta.gov/unemploy/claims.asp), and the DOL economic data page shows no schedule for 2026-12-03 (https://www.dol.gov/newsroom/economicdata). No consensus for the 2026-11-28 week was found and the DOL release text could not be read. The answer would shift toward No if the holiday seasonal factors again push the print down, or if labor-market data keep surprising low; it would shift toward Yes with a rebound toward 195,000 to 200,000, as seen in the weeks before the latest print.
